{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01YaqtGKKXCQ31Aa7HPctU1f","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Architecture and Build Plan Template\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections below in this order. Headings may be renamed slightly to suit the domain, but keep the order and intent. For small systems, a section may be a single sentence. If a section does not apply, keep its heading and give a one-line reason. Prefer tables where the notes suggest them.\n4\t\n5\t---\n6\t\n7\t## 1. Summary\n8\t\n9\tFive to ten sentences or a tight bullet list covering:\n10\t\n11\t- What is being built and for whom.\n12\t- The overall shape of the architecture in one or two sentences.\n13\t- The three to five most important decisions.\n14\t- What the first milestone delivers.\n15\t- The top risks.\n16\t\n17\tSomeone who reads only this section should know what is about to happen and why.\n18\t\n19\t## 2. Context and Goals\n20\t\n21\t- **Problem:** what is painful or missing today, and for whom.\n22\t- **Goals:** the outcomes the system must achieve, in measurable terms where possible.\n23\t- **Non-goals:** things deliberately left out of scope, so nobody assumes they are coming.\n24\t- **Success measures:** how you will know it worked after launch, such as adoption, latency, cost, accuracy, or time saved.\n25\t\n26\t## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n27\t\n28\t- **Ranked quality attributes:** a table with the columns *attribute*, *measurable target*, and *why it matters*, in priority order. Mark targets you inferred as assumptions.\n29\t- **Key functional requirements:** the capabilities that shape the structure. This is not a full backlog.\n30\t- **Constraints:** existing stack, hosting, team size and skills, deadline, budget, compliance, data residency, and mandated vendors.\n31\t- **Hard parts:** the few areas that are new, uncertain, dependent on outside parties, or costly to get wrong, each with one sentence on why.\n32\t\n33\t## 4. Current State\n34\t\n35\tWhat exists today that this work touches: relevant code, services, data stores, infrastructure, and processes. Cite specific files, modules, or systems where you inspected them. Note conventions the plan will follow. For entirely new builds, state what organisational or platform context applies.\n36\t\n37\t## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n38\t\n39\t- **Assumptions:** a table with the columns *assumption*, *impact if wrong*, and *how and when it will be validated*.\n40\t- **Open questions:** each with the owner or person who can answer it, the default you will use if no answer arrives, and the date or milestone by which it must be resolved.\n41\t\n42\t## 6. Architecture Overview\n43\t\n44\t- A text-based diagram (Mermaid or ASCII) showing components, data stores, external systems, and trust boundaries.\n45\t- A short narrative of how the parts fit together.\n46\t- A **component table** with the columns *component*, *responsibility*, *owns which data*, *exposes which interfaces*, *technology*, and *key dependencies*.\n47\t\n48\t## 7. Component Details\n49\t\n50\tFor each significant component:\n51\t\n52\t- Its responsibility and its boundaries, meaning what it explicitly does not do.\n53\t- Its interfaces: whether they are synchronous or asynchronous, the contract format, how they are versioned, and the expected load.\n54\t- Its internal structure, where that matters.\n55\t- How it fails and how it recovers.\n56\t- How it scales, if scale is a driver.\n57\t\n58\tRoutine components can be covered in a line or two.\n59\t\n60\t## 8. Data Design\n61\t\n62\t- The main entities and how they relate to each other.\n63\t- The system of record for each entity, and which component writes to it.\n64\t- Consistency requirements and where transactions are needed.\n65\t- Access patterns and the indexing or partitioning they imply.\n66\t- Retention, deletion, backup, and restore targets.\n67\t- Data classification, covering sensitive fields and how they are protected.\n68\t- How schemas will evolve and how migrations will be done.\n69\t\n70\t## 9. Key Flows\n71\t\n72\tWalk through the two to four most important scenarios step by step, from trigger to outcome. Use sequence diagrams or numbered steps. Include at least one failure path, such as a timeout, retry, duplicate, partial failure, or dependency outage, and show how the system behaves.\n73\t\n74\t## 10. Key Decisions\n75\t\n76\tOne entry per significant decision, optionally as a table:\n77\t\n78\t- **Decision:** what was decided.\n79\t- **Options considered:** at least two realistic ones.\n80\t- **Rationale:** why this option, measured against the ranked drivers.\n81\t- **Reversibility:** whether it is hard or easy to undo.\n82\t- **Revisit if:** the evidence or condition that would reopen the decision.\n83\t\n84\t## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n85\t\n86\tA short subsection for each. Name the concrete mechanism and the milestone in which it is built.\n87\t\n88\t- **Security:** identity, authorisation model, secrets, encryption, input validation, the main threats and their mitigations.\n89\t- **Reliability:** availability and recovery targets, redundancy, timeouts, retries, idempotency, backpressure.\n90\t- **Observability:** logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, alerts tied to user-facing symptoms.\n91\t- **Performance and capacity:** expected load, the bottlenecks you expect, and how they will be load-tested.\n92\t- **Cost:** estimated run cost, the main cost drivers, and the controls on spend.\n93\t- **Operations:** who owns the system, runbooks, on-call expectations, and how support works.\n94\t- **AI-specific concerns, where relevant:** evaluation approach, guardrails, cost and latency budgets, human approval points, and the fallback when the model fails.\n95\t\n96\t## 12. Build Sequence\n97\t\n98\tA milestone table or list. For each milestone:\n99\t\n100\t- **Goal:** the risk it clears or the value it delivers.\n101\t- **Scope:** what is included and what is explicitly excluded.\n102\t- **Deliverables:** the concrete artefacts, features, or environments it produces.\n103\t- **Exit criteria:** checkable conditions that mark it complete.\n104\t- **Dependencies:** what must be finished first, and what can run in parallel.\n105\t- **Rough size:** a range, with the team assumption behind it.\n106\t\n107\tThe first milestone must contain a thin end-to-end slice and the spikes for the highest-risk unknowns. Mark the critical path.\n108\t\n109\t## 13. First Milestone Task Breakdown\n110\t\n111\tA list of concrete tasks. Each one has a verb and a deliverable, its location (module, directory, service, or repository), and a \"done when\" condition. Note the order and which tasks can run in parallel. Spikes include the question being answered, a time box, and the result that would change the plan.\n112\t\n113\t## 14. Testing and Validation Strategy\n114\t\n115\t- Which kinds of tests cover which risks: unit, contract, integration, end-to-end, load, security, and evaluation sets for AI components.\n116\t- The test environments and test data needed.\n117\t- What runs in CI and what blocks a release.\n118\t- How the measurable targets in Section 3 will actually be verified.\n119\t\n120\t## 15. Rollout, Migration, and Rollback\n121\t\n122\t- How the system reaches users: feature flags, staged or percentage rollout, beta groups.\n123\t- For changes to existing systems: how old and new run side by side, the steps for migrating data, and the switchover criteria.\n124\t- The rollback procedure for each risky step, and the point after which rolling back is no longer possible.\n125\t\n126\t## 16. Risks and Mitigations\n127\t\n128\tA table with the columns *risk*, *likelihood*, *impact*, *mitigation*, *early warning sign*, and *owner*. Include technical, delivery, dependency, and organisational risks.\n129\t\n130\t## 17. Deferred Work and Future Evolution\n131\t\n132\t- Items deliberately postponed, and what would trigger building each one.\n133\t- Ways the architecture is expected to evolve, and the extension points that support it.\n134\t- Known shortcuts or technical debt taken on purpose, with a plan to pay each one back.\n135\t\n136\t## 18. Next Steps\n137\t\n138\tThree to seven actions someone can take immediately. These include answering the open questions that block progress and starting the first tasks. Name the specific files, commands, or people where possible.\n139\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"e5c12b54-0b82-467d-8c7d-3efa3c381f35","uuid":"d031e360-570b-49df-a0ab-60fe3491207b","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:21:59.268Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p2ab33809\\skills\\architecture-planner\\reference\\document-template.md","content":"# Architecture and Build Plan Template\n\nUse the sections below in this order. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01DJKzsjErKBzo6dtdLUTTmj","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Planning Guidance and Checklists\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections that are relevant. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n4\t\n5\t## 1. Discovery questions\n6\t\n7\tChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n8\t\n9\t- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n10\t- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n11\t- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n12\t- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n13\t- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n14\t- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n15\t- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n16\t- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n17\t- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n18\t- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n19\t\n20\t## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n21\t\n22\t| Attribute | Express it as |\n23\t|---|---|\n24\t| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n25\t| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n26\t| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n27\t| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n28\t| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n29\t| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n30\t| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n31\t| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n32\t| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n33\t\n34\tIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n35\t\n36\t## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n37\t\n38\t- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n39\t- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n40\t- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n41\t- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n42\t- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n43\t- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n44\t- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n45\t\n46\t## 4. Data checklist\n47\t\n48\t- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n49\t- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n50\t- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n51\t- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n52\t- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n53\t- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n54\t- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n55\t- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n56\t\n57\t## 5. Choosing technology\n58\t\n59\t- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n60\t- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n61\t- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n62\t- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n63\t- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n64\t- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n65\t\n66\t## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n67\t\n68\t- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n69\t- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n70\t- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n71\t- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n72\t- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n73\t- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n74\t- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n75\t\n76\t## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n77\t\n78\tA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n79\t\n80\t- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n81\t- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Map provider groups to the `admin` and `member` roles. Done when an integration test logs in a test user from each group and receives the correct permissions.\"\n82\t- Weak: \"Set up monitoring.\"\n83\t- Strong: \"Emit request count, error rate, and p95 latency per endpoint from the API to the existing metrics stack. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n84\t\n85\tKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n86\t\n87\t## 8. Security checklist\n88\t\n89\t- Identity: how users and services authenticate, and where sessions or tokens are checked.\n90\t- Authorisation: the permission model (roles, attributes, or ownership), enforced on the server side for every request.\n91\t- Secrets: stored in a secret manager, never in code or images, and rotatable.\n92\t- Encryption in transit everywhere. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n93\t- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. Parameterised queries.\n94\t- Least privilege for service accounts, infrastructure roles, and AI tool permissions.\n95\t- Dependency and image scanning in CI. A plan for applying patches.\n96\t- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n97\t- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n98\t\n99\t## 9. Reliability and operations checklist\n100\t\n101\t- A timeout on every network call, retries with backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, and circuit breaking for fragile dependencies.\n102\t- Idempotency keys for operations that may be retried or delivered twice.\n103\t- Backpressure and queue limits, plus dead-letter handling and a process for reprocessing failed messages.\n104\t- Health checks that reflect whether the system can actually serve requests, not just whether the process is running.\n105\t- Alerts based on symptoms users would notice, each linked to a runbook.\n106\t- Structured logs with correlation IDs that can be followed across components.\n107\t- Deployments that are automated, repeatable, and reversible, with an explicit rollback procedure.\n108\t- A capacity plan and a load test at or above the expected peak before launch.\n109\t- Clear ownership: who is on call, how incidents are handled, and who approves changes.\n110\t\n111\t## 10. AI and agentic systems checklist\n112\t\n113\t- **Evaluation first:** a representative, versioned evaluation set with clear pass criteria, run automatically whenever prompts, models, or tools change. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n114\t- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. Add autonomy, planning loops, or multiple agents only when evaluations show they are needed.\n115\t- **Model choice:** weigh quality, latency, cost, context size, and data-handling terms. Keep model access behind an interface so models can be swapped.\n116\t- **Prompts and configuration:** under version control, reviewed, and tied to evaluation results.\n117\t- **Tools:** narrow, well-described interfaces with validated arguments, least-privilege credentials, and dry-run or confirmation modes for actions that can't be undone.\n118\t- **Limits:** a maximum number of steps, a token and spend budget per task, wall-clock timeouts, and loop detection.\n119\t- **Human oversight:** approval points before irreversible or high-impact actions, and a clear way to hand off to a person.\n120\t- **Untrusted input:** treat retrieved documents, tool outputs, and user content as possible injected instructions. Isolate them, and never let them grant new permissions.\n121\t- **Grounding:** for retrieval-based designs, plan how documents are ingested, split into chunks, and refreshed, along with access control on retrieved content and measurement of retrieval quality.\n122\t- **Failure handling:** fallbacks for when the model is slow, unavailable, wrong, or refuses to answer, and degraded modes that still work for users.\n123\t- **Observability:** log inputs, outputs, tool calls, latency, and cost for each step, with redaction of sensitive data. Sample production traffic back into the evaluation set.\n124\t- **Data handling:** what is sent to model providers, how long they keep it, and whether it is allowed to be sent.\n125\t\n126\t## 11. Infrastructure checklist\n127\t\n128\t- All resources defined as code, reviewed, and applied through a pipeline, with no manual changes in production.\n129\t- Environments kept as consistent as possible, with the differences between them stated openly.\n130\t- Remote infrastructure state with locking. State split so a single change can only affect a limited area.\n131\t- Identity, account or project layout, and network design planned first, because they are the hardest to change later.\n132\t- Changes promoted from development to staging to production, with automated checks at each stage.\n133\t- Quotas, limits, and regional capacity checked early.\n134\t- Cost tagging, budgets, and alerts.\n135\t- Backup, disaster recovery, and failover procedures, each tested.\n136\t\n137\t## 12. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n\n## 1. Discovery questions\n\nChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n\n- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n\n## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n\n| Attribute | Express it as |\n|---|---|\n| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n\nIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n\n## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n\n- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n\n## 4. Data checklist\n\n- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n\n## 5. Choosing technology\n\n- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n\n## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n\n- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n\n## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n\nA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n\n- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Done when an integration test logs in a test user from each group and receives the correct permissions.\"\n- Weak: \"Set up monitoring.\"\n- Strong: \"Emit request count, error rate, and p95 latency per endpoint from the API to the existing metrics stack. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n\nKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n\n## 8. A plan for applying patches.\n- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n\n## 9. Old systems that are never retired double the operational cost.\n\n## 13. Common failure modes to check against\n\n- The architecture serves a scale or level of flexibility nobody asked for.\n- Weeks of foundation work with nothing demonstrable at the end.\n- Integration and deployment attempted for the first time near the deadline.\n- Several components writing to the same data, so ownership is unclear.\n- No plan for schema changes, backfills, or rollback.\n- AI behaviour assumed rather than measured.\n- Long-lead dependencies discovered late.\n- Estimates given as single numbers with no stated assumptions.\n- Decisions presented as lists of options with no recommendation.\n","numLines":157,"startLine":1,"totalLines":157}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_jqiqhnwzxu6n7scqtegkjmswyv6di7p3tlcr7klm33zudlxmgkea","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# photoname: Architecture and Build Plan\n\n*A command-line tool that renames a folder of photos by their EXIF capture date*\n\n---\n\n## 1. Summary\n\n- **What:** `photoname` is a cross-platform Python command-line tool. It renames the photos in one folder, along with their related files, to their capture time. For example, `IMG_4021.HEIC` and `IMG_4021.MOV` become `2024-07-14_18-03-22.heic` and `2024-07-14_18-03-22.mov`. *Assumed user:* one technical person, or a few, tidying a personal photo library, mainly on Windows.\n- **Shape:** one Python process that runs **scan → read metadata → plan → preview → apply**. The planner works only in memory and decides every rename before anything on disk changes. The executor then applies that plan and writes a **journal** (a record of every rename) as it goes, so any run can be undone.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. Read metadata with **ExifTool** (a widely used free metadata reader), called once for the whole folder. It sits behind a `MetadataReader` interface. Pure-Python libraries were rejected because HEIC, RAW and video coverage matter more than avoiding an extra install.\n  2. **Dry run is the default.** Nothing changes on disk unless you pass `--apply`.\n  3. **Every apply is journaled, uses two-phase renames, and is all-or-nothing.** If anything fails, the tool rolls the whole run back automatically.\n  4. **Camera clock time is used as recorded.** Photos get no timezone conversion. Only video timestamps, which are stored in UTC, get special handling.\n  5. **Files with no trustworthy date are skipped and listed.** The tool never guesses silently.\n- **First milestone (M1, 2–4 developer-days):** JPEG renaming works end to end, with the preview table, `--apply`, collision suffixes, the journal and `undo`. CI passes on Windows, macOS and Linux. M1 also includes three half-day spikes (short, time-boxed experiments) on formats, filesystems and video time.\n- **Top risks:** overwriting files or losing original names; wrong dates on videos; filesystem quirks such as case-insensitive drives, exFAT SD cards and OneDrive/iCloud placeholder files.\n- **Check this first:** `exiftool \"-FileName<DateTimeOriginal\" -d %Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S%%-c.%%e DIR` already does the basic rename. A custom tool is only worth building for **preview, undo, keeping Live Photo and RAW+JPEG pairs together, and safe re-runs**. If you don't need those, use the one-liner and skip this plan.\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem:** Camera file names (`IMG_4021`, `DSC_0001`, `PXL_2024…`) don't sort by time across devices. They also repeat across cameras and clash when folders are merged. Today the options are renaming by hand or running ExifTool one-liners, which can't be undone and can split Live Photo pairs.\n- **Goals:**\n  - Rename every file that has a reliable capture date to a sortable name: `YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS[_NN].ext`.\n  - Never overwrite or lose a file, and make every run reversible.\n  - Keep related files under the same base name: Live Photo HEIC+MOV pairs, RAW+JPEG pairs, and `.xmp` / `.aae` sidecar files (small files holding edits or metadata).\n  - Make re-runs safe: running the tool again on a finished folder changes nothing.\n- **Non-goals:**\n  - Sorting files into `YYYY/MM` folders.\n  - Searching sub-folders (deferred).\n  - Writing or fixing metadata, including correcting a camera clock (deferred).\n  - Removing duplicates, a GUI, cloud photo libraries, and watching folders for new files.\n- **Success measures:** a 5,000-file mixed folder from the user's own devices renames with no unexplained skips. `undo` then restores exactly the original file listing. The user goes on to run it on the real library.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes**\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it matters |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Data safety | 0 files overwritten or lost. Every rename is recorded in the journal before it happens. `undo` restores the original names exactly. A run interrupted by a crash or power loss can always be recovered. | Original names can't be recovered any other way, and the photos are irreplaceable. |\n| 2 | Date correctness | 100% of the test-corpus files get their expected name. 0 silent guesses: files without a date are skipped and the reason is shown. | A wrong name is worse than no rename, because it gives a false order forever. |\n| 3 | Portability | Runs on Windows 10/11, macOS 13+ and Ubuntu 22.04+, including paths with non-ASCII characters. Install takes 5 minutes or less *(assumption)*. | The user is on Windows, and photos come from mixed devices and drives. |\n| 4 | Performance | Plans 10,000 files in 60 s or less on a local SSD *(assumption)*. | Libraries hold thousands of files. Speed only needs to be bearable. |\n| 5 | Evolvability | A new naming template or date-source rule can be added, with a test, in under an hour. | Naming is a personal preference and likely to change. |\n\n**Key functional requirements**\n\n- Preview the renames, then apply them.\n- Undo a run.\n- Add suffixes when two files would get the same name (for example, burst shots taken in the same second).\n- Group related files and rename them together.\n- Report every skipped file with its reason.\n- Accept a custom naming template.\n\n**Constraints**\n\n- No team was named. *Assumed:* 1 developer who knows Python, working part-time, with no budget.\n- Python 3.11 or later.\n- ExifTool is a runtime dependency. It is free and has a Windows `.exe`.\n\n**Hard parts**\n\n- **Rename safety:**\n  - The original name is the one piece of information you can't get back.\n  - Renames can form chains (A→B while B→C).\n  - On case-insensitive filesystems (Windows, and macOS by default), a change of letter case only (`.JPG` → `.jpg`) needs special handling.\n  - On Linux and macOS, Python's `os.rename` silently overwrites an existing file.\n- **Extracting dates:**\n  - Several date tags can be present: `DateTimeOriginal`, `CreateDate` and `ModifyDate`.\n  - Some files store fractions of a second.\n  - Some files have no EXIF at all, such as screenshots and images sent through WhatsApp.\n  - Video timestamps are stored in UTC, not camera local time.\n- **Grouping related files:** Live Photo and RAW+JPEG pairs must keep matching names, or photo apps stop treating them as pairs.\n- **Platform quirks:**\n  - Paths with non-ASCII characters on Windows have to be passed to ExifTool correctly.\n  - exFAT drives and network (SMB) shares may behave differently on rename.\n  - OneDrive and iCloud placeholder files download themselves when they are read.\n\n## 4. Current State\n\nI inspected the workspace (`w2ed6525f/`). It contains only a `README.md` saying it is intentionally empty, so this is a new build with no existing code or conventions to follow. The plan sets these conventions:\n\n- `src/` layout with `pyproject.toml`\n- pytest for tests and ruff for linting\n- GitHub Actions for CI *(assumption: the code is hosted on GitHub)*\n\n## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n\n**Assumptions**\n\n| # | Assumption | Impact if wrong | How and when validated |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| A1 | Users are technical and can install ExifTool. | If they aren't, the install is a barrier: bundle the `.exe` or switch to a pure-Python reader (see D3). | Ask now. Confirm when the first non-author installs it (M3). |\n| A2 | Inputs are iPhone HEIC + Live Photo MOV, Android JPEG, some RAW (CR2/NEF/ARW/DNG) and MP4. | With no video or RAW, a pure-Python reader would be enough. | Ask now. Check against the S1 test corpus (M1). |\n| A3 | One folder, no sub-folders, on a local disk or USB drive. | Searching sub-folders widens the scope for name clashes. Network shares change how renames behave. | Spike S2 (M1). |\n| A4 | Names follow `YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS`, with lowercase extensions. | Cheap to change, because the template is configurable. | Confirm before M1 ends. |\n| A5 | The camera clock is set to the correct local time, so photo times need no conversion. | Travel photos are named in the camera's time zone. This is usually acceptable. | Open question Q3. |\n| A6 | A folder holds 20,000 files or fewer. | Larger folders may miss the timing target. Memory is still fine. | Performance test (M2). |\n\n**Open questions** (owner for all: the requester)\n\n| # | Question | Default if unanswered | Needed by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Q1 | Which devices and formats are involved? Are there videos or RAW files? | A2 | Start of M2 |\n| Q2 | Is \"install ExifTool separately\" acceptable? | Yes | End of M1 |\n| Q3 | Should files be named in the camera's local time, or converted to one home time zone? | Camera local time | Start of M2 |\n| Q4 | Should files with no EXIF be skipped, or fall back to the file's modified time? | Skip. A `--fallback mtime` flag lets you opt in. | Start of M2 |\n\n## 6. Architecture Overview\n\n```\n user shell:  photoname DIR [--apply] [--format …]     photoname undo DIR\n     │\n┌────▼──────────────── photoname (one Python process) ─────────────────┐\n│  cli ─► scan ─► metadata ─► plan ─► report (dry-run table / summary) │\n│                    │          │                                      │\n│                    │          └─► execute ─► journal (write)         │\n│                    │                 ▲                               │\n│                    │           undo ─┘ (reads journal, probes disk)  │\n└────────────────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┘\n   subprocess, no shell│ argfile + -json   │ os.rename, os.stat\n ═══ trust boundary ═══▼═══════════════════▼═══════════════════════════\n               exiftool binary      DIR/ photos + DIR/.photoname/journal-*.jsonl\n```\n\n**How the parts fit together.** The flow is strictly one-way:\n\n1. `scan` lists the files and groups them by base name (the \"stem\").\n2. `metadata` reads every capture date with a single ExifTool call.\n3. `plan` is pure logic with no input/output. It turns the groups and dates into a validated `Plan`.\n4. `report` prints the plan. With `--apply`, `execute` carries it out and records it in a journal.\n5. `undo` reverses a run using that journal.\n\n**Trust boundary.** File contents and metadata are untrusted. Only date values that pass a strict pattern check ever end up in file names.\n\n**Components**\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Owns data | Interface | Technology | Depends on |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `cli` | Parse arguments, wire the stages together, set exit codes | none | Shell commands; exit codes 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 | `argparse` | all |\n| `scan` | List regular files (skipping symlinks and hidden files) and group by stem | `SourceFile`, `PhotoGroup` | `scan(dir) -> list[PhotoGroup]` | stdlib | — |\n| `metadata` | Get the capture time for each file | `CaptureTime` | `MetadataReader.read(paths) -> dict[path, CaptureTime \\| None]` | ExifTool subprocess | exiftool |\n| `plan` | Choose dates, build names, resolve clashes, detect already-named files, check the plan is safe | `Plan`, `RenameOp`, `Skip` | `build_plan(groups, times, template) -> Plan` | stdlib | — |\n| `report` | Show the dry-run table and summaries | — | `render(plan)` | stdlib | — |\n| `execute` + `journal` | Apply the plan with two-phase renames, roll back on failure, undo | Journal files | `apply(plan)`, `undo(dir)` | stdlib | filesystem |\n\n## 7. Component Details\n\n**`scan`** lists `DIR` without searching sub-folders. It skips symlinks, `.photoname/` and dotfiles. It groups files by stem, ignoring letter case, so `IMG_1.HEIC`, `IMG_1.MOV`, `IMG_1.AAE`, `IMG_1.xmp` and `IMG_1.HEIC.xmp` form one group. In M1 every group holds a single file, but the data shape is already a group so that M2 doesn't need a rewrite. `scan` does not read file contents.\n\n**`metadata` / `ExifToolReader`**\n\n- Makes one subprocess call per run, with no shell, and passes the file paths through an argfile (`-@ file`). This avoids the roughly 32k-character command-line limit on Windows. `-charset filename=utf8` handles non-ASCII paths.\n- Requests these tags: `DateTimeOriginal`, `SubSecTimeOriginal`, `OffsetTimeOriginal`, `CreateDate`, `Keys:CreationDate` (Apple video, which includes the offset), and `QuickTime:CreateDate`, plus `-api QuickTimeUTC`. Spike S1 confirms the exact list.\n- Parses values with a strict pattern (`YYYY:MM:DD HH:MM:SS`). It rejects `0000:00:00` and years before 1990 or in the future, and records which tag supplied the date.\n- **Failure handling:** if ExifTool is missing, the tool exits with code 2 and shows install instructions. The subprocess has a timeout that scales with the number of files. A file that ExifTool can't read returns `None` and is skipped with a reason.\n- The ExifTool version is logged, and a minimum version is set after S1.\n- **Not its job:** this component doesn't build names.\n\n**`plan`** (where the logic lives; pure and heavily tested)\n\n- **Choosing the date:**\n  - For photos: `DateTimeOriginal` (+ subseconds), then `CreateDate`, then skip.\n  - For videos: `Keys:CreationDate` (local time with offset), then `QuickTime:CreateDate` converted from UTC to the machine's local time zone. The second case is flagged `tz_assumed` and shown in the preview.\n  - If `--fallback mtime` is set, the file's modified time is used and labelled as such.\n- **Groups:** the date comes from the primary file in the group, with image preferred over video over RAW. If the members' dates differ by more than 2 s, a warning is shown.\n- **Name:** the date is formatted with `--format` (default `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`), and each member keeps its own extension, lowercased.\n- **Clashes:** groups with the same base name are sorted by (subsecond, original name). The first gets the base name; the rest get `_01`, `_02`, and so on. Clashes are compared ignoring letter case.\n- **Already named:** if a file's current stem already equals `base` or `base_NN` for its own date, it is skipped. This makes re-runs change nothing, and existing names stay stable when new files are added later.\n- **Safety checks (the run aborts if any fails):**\n  - Every target name is unique, ignoring case.\n  - No target matches an existing file that isn't itself being renamed in this plan.\n  - Every target is a single path component with no `/ \\ : * ? \" < > |`.\n  - No target is a Windows reserved name such as `CON` or `NUL`.\n\n**`execute` + `journal`**\n\n1. If `DIR/.photoname/` holds an unfinished journal, refuse to run and tell the user to run `photoname undo DIR`.\n2. Check each source file again (size and modified time). If anything changed since planning, abort.\n3. Write the journal header. It contains every operation (`src`, `tmp`, `target`, and the file's identity: `st_ino`/`st_dev`, falling back to size + mtime). Flush it to disk with `fsync` **once**.\n4. **Phase 1:** rename each `src` to `.<uuid>.photoname-tmp` in the same folder.\n5. **Phase 2:** rename each temp file to its `target`. First check that the target doesn't exist (`os.path.lexists`); on Windows `os.rename` also refuses to overwrite.\n6. Write a `complete` marker.\n\nProgress lines are added to the journal as each rename happens, but they aren't flushed to disk one by one. Recovery doesn't depend on them: `undo` finds each file by checking `src`, `tmp` and `target` against the identity stored in the header. This approach handles chains and avoids around 20,000 disk flushes.\n\n**Failure:** any exception triggers an automatic rollback in reverse order, and the tool exits with code 1. If the rollback itself fails, it exits with code 3 and prints the journal path and the files that need manual attention.\n\n**`undo`** reads the most recent journal. It moves each file back after checking its identity. If something is unclear, such as an unknown file now sitting at the original name, it skips that file and reports it.\n\n**Not its job:** `execute` doesn't make decisions. It only carries out a plan that has already been checked.\n\n## 8. Data Design\n\n- **Entities:**\n  - `SourceFile`: path, extension, size, modified time in nanoseconds, file ID.\n  - `PhotoGroup`: stem, primary file, members.\n  - `CaptureTime`: naive local datetime, subseconds, source tag, `tz_assumed` flag.\n  - `RenameOp`: group, src, tmp, target, identity.\n  - `Plan`: operations, skips with reasons, warnings.\n  - `Journal`: header with `version: 1`, tool version, folder, timestamp and the full list of operations; progress lines; an end marker (`complete` or `rolled_back`).\n- **Where the truth lives:** the filesystem holds the files. Journals are written only by `execute` and read only by `undo`. There is no database.\n- **Consistency:** each run is all-or-nothing.\n- **Retention:** journals stay in `DIR/.photoname/` indefinitely. They are small, about 300 bytes per file. A command to prune them is deferred.\n- **Sensitive data:** photos can contain GPS coordinates and other personal metadata. The tool reads only date tags. Logs and journals contain only file names. Test fixtures have GPS stripped (`exiftool -gps:all=`).\n- **Format changes:** the journal format carries a `version` field, and `undo` refuses versions it doesn't know.\n\n## 9. Key Flows\n\n**F1: Preview (the default).** `photoname D:\\Photos\\2024-trip`\n\n1. Scan finds 1,214 files in 1,180 groups.\n2. One ExifTool call reads all the dates.\n3. The planner produces 1,150 renames, 22 files already named, and 8 skips (5 with no EXIF, 3 unreadable).\n4. The tool prints a table (`old → new`, date source, flags) and the summary.\n5. Nothing on disk changes.\n\nRunning the same command after an apply reports 0 renames.\n\n**F2: Apply.** `photoname D:\\Photos\\2024-trip --apply`\n\n1. The tool rebuilds the plan, prints the summary, and asks `Rename 1,150 files? [y/N]` (`--yes` skips the prompt).\n2. The journal header is written and flushed to disk.\n3. Phase 1 runs, then phase 2, then the `complete` marker is written.\n4. The tool prints: `Renamed 1,150. It reverses every phase-2 rename already done, then every phase-1 rename, using the journal.\n3. The next `photoname DIR` run finds a journal with no end marker and refuses to plan.\n2. `photoname undo DIR` uses the identities in the header to find each file, whether it is at its original name, its temp name or its target. Summary\n\n- **What:** `photoname` is a cross-platform Python command-line tool. It renames the photos in one folder, along with their related files, to their capture time. For example, `IMG_4021.HEIC` and `IMG_4021.MOV` become `2024-07-14_18-03-22.heic` and `2024-07-14_18-03-22.mov`. *Assumed user:* one technical person, or a few, tidying a personal photo library, mainly on Windows.\n- **Shape:** one Python process that runs **scan → read metadata → plan → preview → apply**. The planner works only in memory and decides every rename before anything on disk changes. The executor then applies that plan and writes a **journal** (a record of every rename) as it goes, so any run can be undone.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. Read metadata with **ExifTool** (a widely used free metadata reader), called once for the whole folder. It sits behind a `MetadataReader` interface. Pure-Python libraries were rejected because HEIC, RAW and video coverage matter more than avoiding an extra install.\n  2. **Dry run is the default.** Nothing changes on disk unless you pass `--apply`.\n  3. **Every apply is journaled, uses two-phase renames, and is all-or-nothing.** If anything fails, the tool rolls the whole run back automatically.\n  4. **Camera clock time is used as recorded.** Photos get no timezone conversion. Only video timestamps, which are stored in UTC, get special handling.\n  5. **Files with no trustworthy date are skipped and listed.** The tool never guesses silently.\n- **First milestone (M1, 2–4 developer-days):** JPEG renaming works end to end, with the preview table, `--apply`, collision suffixes, the journal and `undo`. CI passes on Windows, macOS and Linux. M1 also includes three half-day spikes (short, time-boxed experiments) on formats, filesystems and video time.\n- **Top risks:** overwriting files or losing original names; wrong dates on videos; filesystem quirks such as case-insensitive drives, exFAT SD cards and OneDrive/iCloud placeholder files.\n- **Check this first:** `exiftool \"-FileName<DateTimeOriginal\" -d %Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S%%-c.%%e DIR` already does the basic rename. A custom tool is only worth building for **preview, undo, keeping Live Photo and RAW+JPEG pairs together, and safe re-runs**. If you don't need those, use the one-liner and skip this plan.\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem:** Camera file names (`IMG_4021`, `DSC_0001`, `PXL_2024…`) don't sort by time across devices. They also repeat across cameras and clash when folders are merged. Today the options are renaming by hand or running ExifTool one-liners, which can't be undone and can split Live Photo pairs.\n- **Goals:**\n  - Rename every file that has a reliable capture date to a sortable name: `YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS[_NN].ext`.\n  - Never overwrite or lose a file, and make every run reversible.\n  - Keep related files under the same base name: Live Photo HEIC+MOV pairs, RAW+JPEG pairs, and `.xmp` / `.aae` sidecar files (small files holding edits or metadata).\n  - Make re-runs safe: running the tool again on a finished folder changes nothing.\n- **Non-goals:**\n  - Sorting files into `YYYY/MM` folders.\n  - Searching sub-folders (deferred).\n  - Writing or fixing metadata, including correcting a camera clock (deferred).\n  - Removing duplicates, a GUI, cloud photo libraries, and watching folders for new files.\n- **Success measures:** a 5,000-file mixed folder from the user's own devices renames with no unexplained skips. `undo` then restores exactly the original file listing. The user goes on to run it on the real library.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes**\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it matters |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Data safety | 0 files overwritten or lost. Every rename is recorded in the journal before it happens. `undo` restores the original names exactly. A run interrupted by a crash or power loss can always be recovered. | Original names can't be recovered any other way, and the photos are irreplaceable. |\n| 2 | Date correctness | 100% of the test-corpus files get their expected name. 0 silent guesses: files without a date are skipped and the reason is shown. | A wrong name is worse than no rename, because it gives a false order forever. |\n| 3 | Portability | Runs on Windows 10/11, macOS 13+ and Ubuntu 22.04+, including paths with non-ASCII characters. Install takes 5 minutes or less *(assumption)*. | The user is on Windows, and photos come from mixed devices and drives. |\n| 4 | Performance | Plans 10,000 files in 60 s or less on a local SSD *(assumption)*. | Libraries hold thousands of files. Speed only needs to be bearable. |\n| 5 | Evolvability | A new naming template or date-source rule can be added, with a test, in under an hour. | Naming is a personal preference and likely to change. |\n\n**Key functional requirements**\n\n- Preview the renames, then apply them.\n- Undo a run.\n- Add suffixes when two files would get the same name (for example, burst shots taken in the same second).\n- Group related files and rename them together.\n- Report every skipped file with its reason.\n- Accept a custom naming template.\n\n**Constraints**\n\n- No team was named. *Assumed:* 1 developer who knows Python, working part-time, with no budget.\n- Python 3.11 or later.\n- ExifTool is a runtime dependency. It is free and has a Windows `.exe`.\n\n**Hard parts**\n\n- **Rename safety:**\n  - The original name is the one piece of information you can't get back.\n  - Renames can form chains (A→B while B→C).\n  - On case-insensitive filesystems (Windows, and macOS by default), a change of letter case only (`.JPG` → `.jpg`) needs special handling.\n  - On Linux and macOS, Python's `os.rename` silently overwrites an existing file.\n- **Extracting dates:**\n  - Several date tags can be present: `DateTimeOriginal`, `CreateDate` and `ModifyDate`.\n  - Some files store fractions of a second.\n  - Some files have no EXIF at all, such as screenshots and images sent through WhatsApp.\n  - Video timestamps are stored in UTC, not camera local time.\n- **Grouping related files:** Live Photo and RAW+JPEG pairs must keep matching names, or photo apps stop treating them as pairs.\n- **Platform quirks:**\n  - Paths with non-ASCII characters on Windows have to be passed to ExifTool correctly.\n  - exFAT drives and network (SMB) shares may behave differently on rename.\n  - OneDrive and iCloud placeholder files download themselves when they are read.\n\n## 4. Current State\n\nI inspected the workspace (`w2ed6525f/`). It contains only a `README.md` saying it is intentionally empty, so this is a new build with no existing code or conventions to follow. Check against the S1 test corpus (M1). |\n| A3 | One folder, no sub-folders, on a local disk or USB drive. | Searching sub-folders widens the scope for name clashes. Network shares change how renames behave. | Spike S2 (M1). |\n| A4 | Names follow `YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS`, with lowercase extensions. | Cheap to change, because the template is configurable. | Confirm before M1 ends. |\n| A5 | The camera clock is set to the correct local time, so photo times need no conversion. | Travel photos are named in the camera's time zone. This is usually acceptable. | Open question Q3. |\n| A6 | A folder holds 20,000 files or fewer. | Larger folders may miss the timing target. Memory is still fine. | Performance test (M2). |\n\n**Open questions** (owner for all: the requester)\n\n| # | Question | Default if unanswered | Needed by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Q1 | Which devices and formats are involved? Are there videos or RAW files? | A2 | Start of M2 |\n| Q2 | Is \"install ExifTool separately\" acceptable? | Yes | End of M1 |\n| Q3 | Should files be named in the camera's local time, or converted to one home time zone? | Camera local time | Start of M2 |\n| Q4 | Should files with no EXIF be skipped, or fall back to the file's modified time? | Skip. A `--fallback mtime` flag lets you opt in. | Start of M2 |\n\n## 6. Architecture Overview\n\n```\n user shell:  photoname DIR [--apply] [--format …]     photoname undo DIR\n     │\n┌────▼──────────────── photoname (one Python process) ─────────────────┐\n│  cli ─► scan ─► metadata ─► plan ─► report (dry-run table / summary) │\n│                    │          │                                      │\n│                    │          └─► execute ─► journal (write)         │\n│                    │                 ▲                               │\n│                    │           undo ─┘ (reads journal, probes disk)  │\n└────────────────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┘\n   subprocess, no shell│ argfile + -json   │ os.rename, os.stat\n ═══ trust boundary ═══▼═══════════════════▼═══════════════════════════\n               exiftool binary      DIR/ photos + DIR/.photoname/journal-*.jsonl\n```\n\n**How the parts fit together.** The flow is strictly one-way:\n\n1. `scan` lists the files and groups them by base name (the \"stem\").\n2. `metadata` reads every capture date with a single ExifTool call.\n3. `plan` is pure logic with no input/output. It turns the groups and dates into a validated `Plan`.\n4. `report` prints the plan. With `--apply`, `execute` carries it out and records it in a journal.\n5. `undo` reverses a run using that journal.\n\n**Trust boundary.** File contents and metadata are untrusted. Only date values that pass a strict pattern check ever end up in file names.\n\n**Components**\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Owns data | Interface | Technology | Depends on |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `cli` | Parse arguments, wire the stages together, set exit codes | none | Shell commands; exit codes 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 | `argparse` | all |\n| `scan` | List regular files (skipping symlinks and hidden files) and group by stem | `SourceFile`, `PhotoGroup` | `scan(dir) -> list[PhotoGroup]` | stdlib | — |\n| `metadata` | Get the capture time for each file | `CaptureTime` | `MetadataReader.read(paths) -> dict[path, CaptureTime \\| None]` | ExifTool subprocess | exiftool |\n| `plan` | Choose dates, build names, resolve clashes, detect already-named files, check the plan is safe | `Plan`, `RenameOp`, `Skip` | `build_plan(groups, times, template) -> Plan` | stdlib | — |\n| `report` | Show the dry-run table and summaries | — | `render(plan)` | stdlib | — |\n| `execute` + `journal` | Apply the plan with two-phase renames, roll back on failure, undo | Journal files | `apply(plan)`, `undo(dir)` | stdlib | filesystem |\n\n## 7. Component Details\n\n**`scan`** lists `DIR` without searching sub-folders. It skips symlinks, `.photoname/` and dotfiles. It groups files by stem, ignoring letter case, so `IMG_1.HEIC`, `IMG_1.MOV`, `IMG_1.AAE`, `IMG_1.xmp` and `IMG_1.HEIC.xmp` form one group. In M1 every group holds a single file, but the data shape is already a group so that M2 doesn't need a rewrite. `scan` does not read file contents.\n\n**`metadata` / `ExifToolReader`**\n\n- Makes one subprocess call per run, with no shell, and passes the file paths through an argfile (`-@ file`). This avoids the roughly 32k-character command-line limit on Windows. `-charset filename=utf8` handles non-ASCII paths.\n- Requests these tags: `DateTimeOriginal`, `SubSecTimeOriginal`, `OffsetTimeOriginal`, `CreateDate`, `Keys:CreationDate` (Apple video, which includes the offset), and `QuickTime:CreateDate`, plus `-api QuickTimeUTC`. Spike S1 confirms the exact list.\n- Parses values with a strict pattern (`YYYY:MM:DD HH:MM:SS`). It rejects `0000:00:00` and years before 1990 or in the future, and records which tag supplied the date.\n- **Failure handling:** if ExifTool is missing, the tool exits with code 2 and shows install instructions. The subprocess has a timeout that scales with the number of files. A file that ExifTool can't read returns `None` and is skipped with a reason.\n- The ExifTool version is logged, and a minimum version is set after S1.\n- **Not its job:** this component doesn't build names.\n\n**`plan`** (where the logic lives; pure and heavily tested)\n\n- **Choosing the date:**\n  - For photos: `DateTimeOriginal` (+ subseconds), then `CreateDate`, then skip.\n  - For videos: `Keys:CreationDate` (local time with offset), then `QuickTime:CreateDate` converted from UTC to the machine's local time zone. The second case is flagged `tz_assumed` and shown in the preview.\n  - If `--fallback mtime` is set, the file's modified time is used and labelled as such.\n- **Groups:** the date comes from the primary file in the group, with image preferred over video over RAW. If the members' dates differ by more than 2 s, a warning is shown.\n- **Name:** the date is formatted with `--format` (default `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`), and each member keeps its own extension, lowercased.\n- **Clashes:** groups with the same base name are sorted by (subsecond, original name). The first gets the base name; the rest get `_01`, `_02`, and so on. Clashes are compared ignoring letter case.\n- **Already named:** if a file's current stem already equals `base` or `base_NN` for its own date, it is skipped. This makes re-runs change nothing, and existing names stay stable when new files are added later.\n- **Safety checks (the run aborts if any fails):**\n  - Every target name is unique, ignoring case.\n  - No target matches an existing file that isn't itself being renamed in this plan.\n  - Every target is a single path component with no `/ \\ : * ? \" < > |`.\n  - No target is a Windows reserved name such as `CON` or `NUL`.\n\n**`execute` + `journal`**\n\n1. If `DIR/.photoname/` holds an unfinished journal, refuse to run and tell the user to run `photoname undo DIR`.\n2. Check each source file again (size and modified time). If anything changed since planning, abort.\n3. Write the journal header. It contains every operation (`src`, `tmp`, `target`, and the file's identity: `st_ino`/`st_dev`, falling back to size + mtime). Flush it to disk with `fsync` **once**.\n4. **Phase 1:** rename each `src` to `.<uuid>.photoname-tmp` in the same folder.\n5. **Phase 2:** rename each temp file to its `target`. First check that the target doesn't exist (`os.path.lexists`); on Windows `os.rename` also refuses to overwrite.\n6. Write a `complete` marker.\n\nProgress lines are added to the journal as each rename happens, but they aren't flushed to disk one by one. Recovery doesn't depend on them: `undo` finds each file by checking `src`, `tmp` and `target` against the identity stored in the header. This approach handles chains and avoids around 20,000 disk flushes.\n\n**Failure:** any exception triggers an automatic rollback in reverse order, and the tool exits with code 1. If the rollback itself fails, it exits with code 3 and prints the journal path and the files that need manual attention.\n\n**`undo`** reads the most recent journal. It moves each file back after checking its identity. If something is unclear, such as an unknown file now sitting at the original name, it skips that file and reports it.\n\n**Not its job:** `execute` doesn't make decisions. It only carries out a plan that has already been checked.\n\n## 8. Data Design\n\n- **Entities:**\n  - `SourceFile`: path, extension, size, modified time in nanoseconds, file ID.\n  - `PhotoGroup`: stem, primary file, members.\n  - `CaptureTime`: naive local datetime, subseconds, source tag, `tz_assumed` flag.\n  - `RenameOp`: group, src, tmp, target, identity.\n  - `Plan`: operations, skips with reasons, warnings.\n  - `Journal`: header with `version: 1`, tool version, folder, timestamp and the full list of operations; progress lines; an end marker (`complete` or `rolled_back`).\n- **Where the truth lives:** the filesystem holds the files. Journals are written only by `execute` and read only by `undo`. There is no database.\n- **Consistency:** each run is all-or-nothing.\n- **Retention:** journals stay in `DIR/.photoname/` indefinitely. They are small, about 300 bytes per file. A command to prune them is deferred.\n- **Sensitive data:** photos can contain GPS coordinates and other personal metadata. The tool reads only date tags. Logs and journals contain only file names. Test fixtures have GPS stripped (`exiftool -gps:all=`).\n- **Format changes:** the journal format carries a `version` field, and `undo` refuses versions it doesn't know.\n\n## 9. Key Flows\n\n**F1: Preview (the default).** `photoname D:\\Photos\\2024-trip`\n\n1. Scan finds 1,214 files in 1,180 groups.\n2. One ExifTool call reads all the dates.\n3. The planner produces 1,150 renames, 22 files already named, and 8 skips (5 with no EXIF, 3 unreadable).\n4. The tool prints a table (`old → new`, date source, flags) and the summary.\n5. Nothing on disk changes.\n\nRunning the same command after an apply reports 0 renames.\n\n**F2: Apply.** `photoname D:\\Photos\\2024-trip --apply`\n\n1. The tool rebuilds the plan, prints the summary, and asks `Rename 1,150 files? [y/N]` (`--yes` skips the prompt).\n2. The journal header is written and flushed to disk.\n3. Phase 1 runs, then phase 2, then the `complete` marker is written.\n4. The tool prints: `Renamed 1,150. Undo with: photoname undo D:\\Photos\\2024-trip`.\n\n**F3: Failure — a file is locked on Windows.** During phase 2, `IMG_0042.tmp → 2024-07-14_18-03-22.jpg` raises `PermissionError` because the image is open in another app.\n\n1. `execute` stops at once.\n2. It reverses every phase-2 rename already done, then every phase-1 rename, using the journal.\n3. It writes `rolled_back` to the journal and exits with code 1: `Rolled back; close the program using IMG_0042.jpg and re-run.`\n\nThe folder is now exactly as it was before the run.\n\n**F4: Failure — interrupted by power loss or killing the process.**\n\n1. The next `photoname DIR` run finds a journal with no end marker and refuses to plan.\n2. `photoname undo DIR` uses the identities in the header to find each file, whether it is at its original name, its temp name or its target. It moves each one back and reports any file it couldn't place.\n\n## 10. Key Decisions\n\n| # | Decision | Options considered | Rationale (by driver) | Reversibility | Revisit if |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| D1 | Build a tool rather than document an ExifTool one-liner | One-liner; small script; this tool | The one-liner has no preview, undo or grouping, and does unclear things on re-runs. These gaps hit drivers 1 and 2. | Easy | The user doesn't care about undo or grouping. In that case, ship the one-liner. |\n| D2 | Python 3.11+ | Python; Go or Rust single binary | Fastest to build, `pipx install` works on all three platforms, and it's assumed to be the developer's language. A single binary only helps if users can't install Python. | Hard (language) | A1 is wrong and users need a single download. Then reconsider Go plus bundled ExifTool. |\n| D3 | ExifTool behind a `MetadataReader` interface | ExifTool; pure Python (Pillow + pillow-heif, exifread) | ExifTool reliably covers HEIC, CR3, MOV and MP4 (driver 2). Pure-Python options don't cover video or CR3. The cost is an extra install (driver 3), so the interface keeps a pure-Python reader possible later. | Medium | Q1 shows no video or RAW, or S1 finds Windows path problems that can't be fixed. |\n| D4 | Journal + two-phase rename + all-or-nothing rollback | Direct renames, best effort; skip failed files and continue | Simplest model that guarantees driver 1. It handles chains and case-only changes. Partial success would complicate both clash handling and undo. | Medium | Users regularly hit locked files on large folders and want to continue past them. |\n| D5 | Dry run by default, `--apply` to rename | Apply with a confirmation prompt; dry run by default | Safe by default, and the preview is the main feature. | Easy | Users find it annoying. Then add a `--yes` alias or a config setting. |\n| D6 | Camera local time, no conversion for photos | Convert everything to one home time zone | EXIF often has no time-zone offset, so converting would mean guessing. Matches what most photo tools do. | Easy (only the planner rule changes) | Q3 answer says otherwise. |\n| D7 | Skip files with no EXIF date; mtime fallback only by opt-in | Always fall back to mtime | A file's modified time changes when it's copied, so it's often wrong. This protects driver 2. | Easy | Q4 answer says otherwise. |\n| D8 | First file keeps the base name; clashes get `_NN` | Suffix every member of a clash; use subsecond digits in the name | Existing names stay stable when new files are added, which makes re-runs safe. | Medium (changes names users see) | — |\n| D9 | `argparse`, journal stored in `DIR/.photoname/` | Typer/Click; journal in the user's data folder | No dependencies, and the journal travels with the folder (for example, on a USB drive). | Easy | — |\n\n## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n\n- **Security** (local tool, single user, built in M1):\n  - ExifTool runs without a shell, and paths are passed through an argfile, so there is no command injection.\n  - EXIF strings never flow into names; only parsed date digits do.\n  - The `--format` output is checked to be a single safe path component, which prevents path traversal.\n  - Symlinks are never followed.\n  - Dependency scanning: `pip-audit` in CI (M1).\n- **Reliability:** covered by D4 and §7. All-or-nothing runs, recovery by checking file identity, an ExifTool timeout, a re-check of each file before applying, and refusal to run while an unfinished journal exists (M1).\n- **Observability:**\n  - The dry-run table and summary.\n  - `-v` writes structured log lines to stderr.\n  - The journal acts as an audit trail.\n  - `--json` outputs the plan as JSON (M3).\n  - Clear exit codes: 0 success, 1 rolled back, 2 setup or usage error, 3 manual action needed.\n- **Performance:** the bottleneck is ExifTool reading files, about 20–40 s for 10,000 files *(estimate, measured in S1 and M2)*. If needed, the `-fast2` option reads less of each file. Renames are cheap. Memory is under 50 MB for 20,000 files.\n- **Cost:** none to run. ExifTool and Python are free.\n- **Operations:** the user runs the tool themselves, so there is no on-call. The README has a \"something went wrong\" section: run `undo`, explain exit code 3, and say how to read the journal (M3).\n- **AI-specific concerns:** not applicable; no model is involved.\n\n## 12. Testing and Validation Strategy\n\n- **Unit and property tests** (`plan`, `scan`, parsers): cover the date and naming rules (driver 2), safety checks and re-run behaviour (driver 1). They use Hypothesis to generate random sets of names and dates, including clashes and chains.\n- **Fault-injection tests** (`execute`): an `os.rename` failure at every step, and a kill at a random step followed by `undo`. These guard driver 1 and block any release.\n- **Integration tests with real ExifTool:**\n  - Generated fixtures: tiny files tagged by ExifTool.\n  - A golden corpus from M2 onward: one real sample per format from A2, GPS stripped, cloned and re-tagged to create edge cases. The expected names live in `tests/fixtures/expected.json`.\n- **Cross-platform:** the CI matrix runs on Windows, macOS and Linux for driver 3. The exFAT and SMB results come from the S2 manual run.\n- **Performance:** `scripts/make_corpus.py` generates 10,000 tagged JPEGs, and a manual timing is recorded in M2 (driver 4). This doesn't block CI.\n- **What blocks a release:** ruff, every pytest suite on all three OSes, and pip-audit with no high-severity findings.\n\n## 15. Rollout, Migration, and Rollback\n\n- **Rollout:**\n  1. The author runs it on a *copy* of a real folder (M2 exit).\n  2. Then on the real library.\n  3. Then shares it through `pipx install git+…@v0.x`, moving to PyPI in M3.\n- **Migration:** none; no older system exists.\n- **Rolling back renames:** `photoname undo DIR`. The point of no return is deleting `.photoname/`, or moving or renaming files by hand after a run. `undo` detects this through the identity check and reports the files it can't restore instead of guessing.\n- **Rolling back the tool itself:** `pipx install photoname==<previous>`. Journals with a version number keep older journals readable.\n\n## 16. Risks and Mitigations\n\n| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation | Early warning | Owner |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| A bug overwrites a file or loses original names | Low | Severe | D4, no-overwrite check, fault-injection and property tests, dry run by default | Any failure in the T9 tests | Developer |\n| Video dates are off by hours (UTC vs local) | Medium | Medium | Spike S3, prefer `Keys:CreationDate`, `tz_assumed` flag shown in preview | The Live Photo MOV time differs from its HEIC | Developer |\n| Windows non-ASCII paths break the ExifTool call | Medium | High | Argfile + `-charset filename=utf8`, S1, CI fixture with a Unicode path | S1 result | Developer |\n| exFAT drives, network shares or OneDrive/iCloud placeholders behave unexpectedly | Medium | Medium | S2; warn when a folder looks cloud-synced; document unsupported filesystems | S2 results table | Developer |\n| ExifTool install puts users off (A1) | Medium (if users are non-technical) | Medium | Per-OS install guide; the D3 interface allows a pure-Python reader | First outside user's feedback in M3 | Requester |\n| Scope creep (folder sorting, sub-folders, clock shift) | Medium | Low | Non-goals and deferred list kept explicit | New requests during M2 | Requester |\n\n## 17. Deferred Work and Future Evolution\n\n- **Deferred:**\n  - `--recursive` (when the user has nested folders; clashes would be resolved per folder).\n  - `--shift +1h` to correct a camera clock (when travel photos come up).\n  - Sorting into `YYYY/MM` folders.\n  - Pruning journals.\n  - A pure-Python reader (if A1 or Q1 points that way).\n  - A persistent ExifTool process (`-stay_open`), if performance falls short.\n- **Extension points:** the `MetadataReader` interface (new backends), the date-choice rule list in `plan` (new date sources), the `--format` template (new naming styles) and the journal `version` field.\n- **Deliberate shortcuts:**\n  - All-or-nothing apply. Pay it back with \"skip and continue\" if locked files become common.\n  - The file-ID check has no file-contents hash. Add one if S2 shows the file ID is unstable on exFAT.\n\n## 18.
